title: Here There Are Blueberries by Moisés Kaufman and Amanda Gronich on Br...
transcript: When a photo album from Auschwitz lands on Rebecca Erbelding's desk at the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, everyone is more surprised by what it doesn't show than what it does. There are no victims in any of the photographs. As these historians dig into it further, a disturbingly mundane impression emerges, one that captures the everyday lives of the people responsible for some of the worst acts recorded in human history. One series of photos, captioned “here there are blueberries,” depicts a group of young women leisurely enjoying a refreshing snack at what was essentially the weekend getaway spot for Nazis and their families. This play follows the investigation into this photo album, using interviews, among other primary sources, to take you on a consistently intriguing and sometimes harrowing psychological journey. It's virtually the same production as what was presented at New York Theatre Workshop in 2024, though they've made some casting changes — not all of which are for the better, in my opinion. Nevertheless, everyone does a solid job enhancing the material with subtle characterizations, without upstaging the text itself. After all, this is primarily a documentary piece, with elements of lecture and drama baked in — its construction certainly reflects journalistic instincts from its writing team. The methodical sequencing and pacing maximizes the impact of the questions it raises around human tendencies and our own culpability — in a theoretical sense when looking back at the Holocaust, or more broadly as bystanders and drones with respect to any other atrocities, including those we're witnessing right now. As an illustration of how pervasive depravity can be when normalized or compartmentalized, Here There Are Blueberries is a refreshingly unique and urgent theatrical experience, especially for Broadway these days.
